 Note to Jim Chalmers: Rein in Labor's outrageous net zero spend-a-thon before even thinking about a GST hike
 Labor wouldn't need to consider increasing GST if it wasn't running Australia into the ground with net zero zealotry and poorly conceived social welfare policy, writes Caroline Di Russo.
 Caroline Di Russo News24.com.au Contributor and Political Commentator 3 min read October 22, 2026 - 5:00AM News24 Media Watch Dog Columnist Gerard Henderson reacts to ABC host Sally Sara's soft interview with Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Every year, someone flies a kite about changing the GST.
 The flight is usually short, but it reliably tests the country’s appetite for tax reform.
 The latest offering is from Grattan Institute chief executive Aruna Sathanapally, calling for an increase in the GST rate from 10 to 15 per cent and an expansion to all food products.
 Sathanapally - who Treasurer Jim Chalmers handpicked to present at his economic reform roundtable in August - claims the changes would raise about $76 billion of additional GST annually.
 The sweetener is income tax cuts for low and middle income earners and higher welfare payments.
 Lovely chit chat, but the cart is firmly before the horse.
 Before anyone talks about increasing tax revenue, there must be a serious conversation about government spending.
 CEO of the Grattan Institute Aruna Sathanapally during a Tax Reform Roundtable at Parliament House in Canberra in July. Picture: NewsWire/ Martin Ollman Put simply, if government spends better, it does not need to raise as much from Australians who are already skinned by layers of taxation levied on pretty much everything that moves and plenty that does not.
 Despite this already enormous individual tax burden, the Albanese Labor government is well versed in scouting around for new honey pots while throwing billions at the wall and achieving only the vaguest of outcomes for the country.
 It is probably too kind to suggest there are vague outcomes.
 Often, it is hard to see how there is any positive outcome at all.
 Spending under this government has been wildly out of control and poorly prioritised from the get-go.
 Labor’s obsession with net zero is running the country into the ground and forcing the government to put heavy industry on financial life support.
 See Tomago.
 See also the NDIS, a social policy that is demand driven and not means tested, now a haemorrhaging line item in the budget.
 From inception, the NDIS was a financial disaster waiting to happen and is now totally unmanageable and unsustainable.
 The government has pretended to rein it in, but its efforts resemble the moving of the proverbial deck chairs.
 Then there’s the smaller spending fluff that accumulates over time: climate Schoolies in Fiji, $2 million spent renovating the Greens’ party room, ministers gorging themselves on taxpayer junkets while wanting on performance.
 Treasurer Jim Chalmers speaks to the media at Parliament House, Canberra. Picture: NewsWire/ Hilary Wardhaugh These are not massive sums in isolation, but they add up, and they are symptomatic of a government with no understanding of the real economy and no respect for how hard a dollar is earned in that real economy.
 Disappointingly but unsurprisingly, reform proposals usually focus on increasing overall tax revenue because it’s easier to tax more to fill budget blackholes than tidy up the blackholes themselves.
 It’s an aged old game of voter arithmetic - who can you take from, who can you give it to, and what is the net electoral benefit to the government.
 Rarely does the net benefit to the country get taken into consideration.
 As for the proposed reform, there is merit in shifting the tax burden from income to consumption.
 Australia’s income tax is unusually burdensome and should be reduced.
 However, this can only properly be done through the indexation of tax brackets.
 That should be the first port of call.
 Without indexation, any income tax cut is quickly inflated out of existence as bracket creep soaks up the gains, especially in a high inflation environment.
 Also, rather than increasing the GST and expanding it to all food products, simply broadening the base may be neater.
 Anyone who has ever coded transactions for a Business Activity Statement - as I have - knows the current GST rules are stunningly inconsistent and an administrative minefield.
 The uneven application of GST can also make cashflow management difficult for business.
 For example, in hospitality you buy fresh items with no GST and sell items with GST, so you collect a large sum of GST with very little offset.
 Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres denies there’s any friction between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers, calling the Labor government “very stable”. 
“This is a cabinet-style government that’s working very well; it's very stable,” Mr Ayres told News24 Political Editor Andrew Clennell. 
“It’s a real contrast to not only what’s happening around the world, but a real contrast to what's happening on the other side of politics.
“Which is a total mess and has been since 2013.” Broadening the GST base would alleviate some administrative burden and improve productivity because every hour a business spends mucking around with regulation is an hour not spent on the tools.
 It’s also worth noting that even with greater GST revenue, the budget will still likely remain in deficit.
 The latest Intergenerational Report predicts deficits for the next 40 years.
 In that case, any income tax cuts would still likely be funded by debt rather than by the additional revenue.
 News24 host Steve Price says Treasurer Jim Chalmers is trying to “bluff his way through” and pretend there is no problem with the Australian economy. The proposed corresponding tax cuts are not the affordable result of a higher tax take; they are simply the carrot to entice voters into accepting a higher consumption tax.
 It’s good electoral maths rather than actual maths.
 In the end, this proposal is just the latest GST thought bubble.
 What Australia needs before further reform is a change in attitude towards fiscal discipline and how the burden of taxation is spread across all Australians.
 On the spending side, we must demand that government focuses on producing value for Australians rather than wallpapering over poor government decisionâ€‘making by taxing more from the productive sections of society.
 Until that conversation is had, and until spending is brought under control, the government has no business looking outwards to the taxpayer for another dollar.
 Caroline Di Russo is a lawyer with 15 years of experience specialising in commercial litigation and corporate insolvency and since February 2023 has been the Liberal Party President in Western Australia.
